h1: The 7 Best Corded Electric Leaf Blowers of 2026, Ranked & Reviewed
metaTitle: Best Corded Leaf Blowers 2026: Ranked & Reviewed
metaDescription: Ranked and reviewed by Primea: 7 corded electric leaf blowers scored on airflow, 12 to 13 amp motors, 3-in-1 versatility and value, from 180 to 700 CFM.
summary: The SENIX 12 AMP is the corded blower to buy: 700 CFM, the highest airflow in this ranking, at a price under $50. The WORX 12 Amp Turbine is the better-balanced daily tool if you clear leaves every week. For one tool that also vacuums and mulches, the WORX Trivac 600 CFM is the pick. Skip the 180 CFM BLACK+DECKER unless your yard is a patio and a strip of lawn.
intro: A corded blower is limited less by its motor than by the extension cord you plug it into. Run a 12 amp tool down a long, thin cord and voltage sags before it reaches the fan, so a blower rated for 700 CFM at the wall can feel like a much weaker machine at the far fence. Most owners blame the blower. The cord is usually the culprit, and no listing mentions it.

We ranked seven corded electric blowers from WORX, SENIX, Grasstigon and BLACK+DECKER on the Primea framework, weighting airflow, handling and value most heavily. The spread is wide, from 180 CFM up to 700 CFM, and so is the job each one suits. Cordless and gas machines were left out on purpose, because choosing a cord changes what you should care about.

products.name: SENIX 12 AMP Corded Electric Leaf Blower
products.verdict: The most airflow in the ranking at a bargain tier. Hard to argue with on paper.
products.description:
SENIX pairs a 12 amp motor with a 700 CFM rating, the highest airflow figure of the seven blowers here. In a corded tool, amperage is the ceiling on power, so a full 12 amp draw is what you want before you look at anything else.

It sits above the WORX 12 Amp Turbine because it claims 100 more CFM while landing in the cheaper $25 to $50 bracket. The trade is brand depth: WORX has a larger service and parts network, and SENIX does not list the mulching or vacuum modes the Trivac offers.

Buy it for wet autumn leaves on a mid-sized lot where raw push matters most. The caveat is that CFM says nothing about air speed, and the listing gives no weight, so confirm it feels balanced before a long session.
products.idealFor: Mid-sized yards where moving wet leaves quickly is the priority.
products.skipIf: You want a combined blower, vacuum and mulcher in one tool.

products.name: WORX 12 Amp Turbine Electric Leaf Blower for Daily Leaf Removal
products.verdict: A turbine-style 12 amp WORX built for regular use, with 600 CFM behind it.
products.description:
WORX builds this one around a turbine fan and a 12 amp motor rated at 600 CFM, and the name says it is meant for daily leaf removal. A turbine generally gives a steadier, more focused stream than a basic axial fan, which helps when you are chasing a pile along a fence line.

It ranks second, 100 CFM below the SENIX, because paper airflow favors the cheaper tool. What you get for the extra spend is a brand that stocks replacement parts and a design aimed at repeated use rather than a one-weekend clearout.

Choose it if you blow the yard every few days and want a tool built around that routine. Note that the facts we have list no weight or cord length, so check both on the listing, since a heavy front end tires wrists over a half hour.
products.idealFor: Owners who clear leaves every few days through the season.
products.skipIf: You only blow the yard once or twice a year.

products.name: Grasstigon 13A Electric Leaf Blower Corded
products.verdict: The only 13 amp motor here, matching the WORX Turbine at 600 CFM.
products.description:
The Grasstigon 13A is the only blower in this group with a 13 amp motor, one amp above the SENIX and WORX units, and it delivers 600 CFM in a handheld body. More current can mean a bit more headroom under load, though a rating is not a guarantee.

It lands third because it matches the WORX Turbine's airflow at the same $50 to $100 tier while carrying the weaker name recognition. The SENIX out-pushes it by 100 CFM for less money, which is the honest reason it is not higher.

A good fit for buyers who want a spec edge and do not mind a newer brand. The caveat is support: if the switch or cord fails, you are relying on the seller rather than a service network.
products.idealFor: Buyers who prioritize motor rating and handheld simplicity.
products.skipIf: You want a long established warranty and parts network.

products.name: WORX Trivac 3-in-1 Electric Leaf Blower/Leaf Vacuum/Leaf Mulcher
products.verdict: Blows, vacuums and mulches at 600 CFM. The yard-cleanup Swiss army knife.
products.description:
This Trivac listing is the 600 CFM version of WORX's three-in-one: a blower, a leaf vacuum and a mulcher in one corded body. Mulching shreds leaves down so a pile fills far fewer bags, which matters when the collection day limit is tight.

It ranks fourth because a multi-mode tool compromises. Pure blowers like the SENIX hand you 100 CFM more in a lighter, simpler shell, and you pay a convenience tax of switching modes. Against the 350 CFM Trivac below it, this is the clear choice for real blowing duty.

Best for small to mid-sized yards where bagging leaves is the chore. The caveat is that vacuum mode is slower and heavier to carry than blowing, so expect it to feel like work on large lawns.
cons: Vacuum mode tiring on big lawns
products.idealFor: Owners who bag leaves and want fewer trips to the curb.
products.skipIf: You only blow leaves into a pile and never vacuum.

products.name: Grasstigon Electric Leaf Blower Corded
products.verdict: A 390 CFM budget handheld that moves dry leaves without fuss.
products.description:
The standard Grasstigon corded blower puts out 390 CFM from a handheld body and sits in the $25 to $50 tier. That is roughly double the BLACK+DECKER's airflow, which is the gap between pushing a pile and merely nudging it.

It ranks fifth because the 13A Grasstigon above gives you 600 CFM for a modest step up, and the SENIX gives 700 CFM at this same price. Where it earns its slot is as the sensible middle ground for people who find those two overkill.

Pick it for a small lawn with dry leaves and a short run to an outlet. Skip it for wet, matted leaves: at this airflow they will stall rather than lift.
cons: SENIX gives more CFM, same price
products.idealFor: Small lawns with dry leaves and an outlet close by.
products.skipIf: You regularly face wet, matted leaf drifts.

products.name: WORX Trivac 3-in-1 Electric Leaf Blower/Leaf Vacuum/Leaf Mulcher
products.verdict: The older, 350 CFM Trivac. Fine for tidy lawns, weak for anything bigger.
products.description:
This is the 350 CFM Trivac, the lower-airflow sibling of the 600 CFM unit. It keeps the same blower, vacuum and mulcher trio, and sits in the same $50 to $100 bracket, which is where the ranking problem starts.

It placed sixth because the 600 CFM Trivac costs in the same tier and nearly doubles the airflow, leaving little reason to pick this one unless it is on sale. Its mulching feature is the draw, since few blowers around 350 CFM offer one.

A reasonable buy for a townhouse yard or a few trees, where mulching makes bagging easy. The caveat is plain: 350 CFM struggles with wet leaves, and the identical product name makes it easy to order the wrong version by mistake.
cons: Roughly half the newer Trivac airflow
Same price tier as better model
Easy to confuse with 600 CFM listing
products.idealFor: Tiny yards with a few trees that need bagging.
products.skipIf: You can find the 600 CFM Trivac in the same price range.

products.name: BLACK+DECKER Electric Leaf Blower
products.verdict: A light 180 CFM sweeper for patios and decks, not for leaf piles.
products.description:
BLACK+DECKER's corded blower delivers 180 CFM from a handheld body in the $25 to $50 tier. At that airflow it is a sweeper, good at clearing dust, grass clippings and light debris off hard surfaces.

It ranks last because every other tool here moves at least double the air. The 390 CFM Grasstigon costs the same and clears real leaf cover, so this model only wins on brand familiarity and a likely lighter feel.

The right buyer has a patio, a deck or a driveway to tidy and does not want to haul anything heavy. The caveat is capacity: pointed at a lawn full of oak leaves, it will take far longer than any rival on this list.
products.idealFor: Patios, decks and driveways with light debris.
products.skipIf: You have trees that drop leaves across a full lawn.

methodology.title: Airflow rating
methodology.description: We compared stated CFM across all seven blowers and rewarded real push at the wall, while noting that CFM alone does not describe how focused the stream is.

methodology.title: Motor draw
methodology.description: Corded power is capped by amperage, so 12 and 13 amp motors were weighted above lower or unlisted ratings.

methodology.title: Versatility
methodology.description: Blower-vacuum-mulcher combinations earned credit for replacing extra tools, offset by the weight and mode-switching they add.

methodology.title: Value per dollar
methodology.description: Airflow against price tier decided the order between close rivals, since similar CFM at a lower bracket wins.

methodology.title: Support and clarity
methodology.description: Brands with parts networks and unambiguous model listings scored higher than ones with thin support or confusing duplicate names.

whatMatters.factor: CFM, and what it leaves out
whatMatters.detail: CFM measures the volume of air a blower moves per minute. It tells you how much a machine can shift at once, which matters for heavy, wet leaves. It does not capture air speed, so a high-CFM tool with a wide nozzle can still feel gentle. Compare CFM on the listing, then look for nozzle shape.

Because a corded blower has no battery, its amp rating is the power ceiling. Twelve amps is the typical full-power household draw, and thirteen is the most you will see on a standard outlet. A listing that omits amps is hiding something, so look for the number in the title or spec box.

A thin or very long cord drops voltage, which weakens the fan. Heavy-gauge cords carry current with less loss, so a 700 CFM blower stays closer to its rating at the end of the run. Check the cord you own: a flimsy light-duty cord defeats a strong motor.

Three-in-one blowers like the WORX Trivac pull leaves into a bag and shred them. That shrinks the pile, which helps where yard waste pickup limits volume. The cost is weight and slower work. Check whether the listing includes a collection bag and how mode changes happen.

A handheld blower is held out front for the whole job, so a heavy motor housing tires the wrist fast. Listings often skip weight, so read the product details or Q&A. A lighter tool at 390 CFM sometimes finishes a yard faster than a heavy one at 700 CFM because you keep working longer.

howToChoose.intro: Match the CFM to the leaf load you face, not to the biggest number on the page.

faq.q: What extension cord should I use with a corded leaf blower?
faq.a: Use a heavy-gauge outdoor cord, and keep it as short as the job allows. A thin cord causes voltage drop, which cuts the fan speed on 12 and 13 amp models like the SENIX 12 AMP and Grasstigon 13A.

faq.q: What is the most common mistake when buying a corded blower?
faq.a: Chasing CFM alone. The SENIX leads at 700 CFM, but a heavy tool you tire of holding clears less than a lighter Grasstigon at 390 CFM. Check weight, cord needs and leaf type before the number.

faq.q: Is a 3-in-1 worth it over a plain blower?
faq.a: Only if you bag leaves. The WORX Trivac 600 CFM mulches and vacuums, cutting the volume you haul away. If you blow leaves into a corner or onto a tarp, the lighter SENIX or WORX Turbine does the job faster.

faq.q: How do I tell the two WORX Trivac listings apart?
faq.a: They share a name, so check the airflow line. One is 350 CFM and the other is 600 CFM. Both sit in the $50 to $100 tier, so the 600 CFM version is nearly always the better buy.

faq.q: How do I maintain a corded blower?
faq.a: Clear leaf debris from the intake after each session, wipe the housing and coil the cord loosely rather than tight. Check the cord for nicks before plugging in. On the WORX Trivac, empty the bag and clear the mulching chamber.

faq.q: Can a corded blower handle wet leaves?
faq.a: It can, but only the strongest do it well. The SENIX at 700 CFM and the 600 CFM WORX and Grasstigon units can lift damp leaves. The 180 CFM BLACK+DECKER and 350 CFM Trivac will stall on matted piles.

finalTake: For most yards, buy the SENIX 12 AMP: it has the highest airflow here at a bargain price. Step up to the WORX 12 Amp Turbine if you blow the lawn weekly and value parts support. Take the WORX Trivac 600 CFM if bagging and mulching leaves is your real chore. Leave the 180 CFM BLACK+DECKER for patios, and buy a good extension cord regardless.
